title: Effects of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn on the Technological Properties of AlSi7Mg0.3 (A356) Casting Alloy
abstract: Abstract With increasing use of secondary material certain alloying elements may accumulate over repeated melting cycles. To determine the influence of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn on the technological properties of AlSi7Mg0.3 cast alloy three compositions with varying additions of these elements to a primary alloy melt were produced. Gravity die-casting experiments using a tensile sample permanent mold were conducted, and the cast samples ran through a heat treatment to achieve practical properties. All samples passed through X-ray analysis to minimize the influence of defects on mechanical properties. Specimen for mechanical testing, microscopic analysis and corrosion tests were taken from the cast samples. Quasi-static mechanical properties were measured via tensile and hardness testing, whereas dynamic mechanical properties were determined with high-speed tensile tests. Furthermore, various cyclic fatigue tests are conducted to derive comprehensive S–N curves for each composition. A small increase in   R p 0,2  (YS) but a clear decrease in   A 5  (Elongation) for quasi-static, as well as for dynamic tensile tests is detected with higher Fe- and Mn-proportions. The further addition of higher amounts of Cu and Zn also affects the mechanical properties in a similar way, albeit at a lower scale. However, Cu significantly aggravates the corrosion properties, whereas no such effect could be detected for Fe and Mn. On the other hand, fatigue properties were not as strongly affected by higher Fe and Mn amounts. In total, the results of this study present a comprehensive overview of the effects that higher amounts of accumulating alloying elements have on the technological properties of AlSi7Mg0.3 cast alloy.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A focus of recent development in the non-ferrous metal industry is on increasing the proportion of secondary metal, especially secondary aluminum. As aluminum is a rather base metal, more noble alloying elements, especially Fe, Cu, Mn and Zn, are accumulating during repeated remelting processes. 1  This leads to a continued downcycling of aluminum alloys if no neat sorting of the various alloys occurs. 2  Due to this, aluminum foundries prefer to use primary and laboriously purified alloys supplied by smelting plants rather than melting scrap directly in their facilities. Therefore, the full potential of secondary aluminum is not exploited. Current understanding indicates that various alloying elements can adversely affect the technological properties of aluminum alloys, depending on their concentrations in specific alloys 3 . While industry standards provide guidelines for acceptable chemical compositions, the specific effects of each detrimental element on the material properties are often unclear.

Al-Si alloys with elevated Cu contents offer high strength and toughness, particularly at room and elevated temperatures, with optimal mechanical strength found at a copper content of 1.5 m% based on an Al 7 m% Si alloy. 9   However, these alloys are susceptible to solidification cracks and stress corrosion cracking, necessitating precise casting techniques. Copper, moreover, enhances mechanical properties at higher temperatures. 10

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: This study focuses on the determination of the influence of particularly critical elements on the properties of the widespread AlSi7Mg0.3 casting alloy. The chemical composition and further details are specified in DIN EN 1706 3  as shown in Table  1 . Additional levels of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn were selected to represent the typical impurity profile of the available scrap feedstock. In view of state-of-the-art sorting technologies, expected contaminant levels were assumed in a conservative manner. sections.heading: Design of Experiment and Set up
paragraphs: To define the influence of the accumulating alloying elements a systematic experimental plan was developed to conduct a sensitivity analysis regarding microstructure, corrosion behavior and mechanical properties of gravity die cast AlSi7Mg0.3. A first outlook on this study is presented in Bleicher et al. 16  The selection of investigated elements and their respective amounts added were determined by inquiries on the nature and composition of Al scrap, which usually accrues. 2 , 17  The experimental design, as shown in Table  2 , is therefore simulating an increasing amount of several elements in the Al alloy due to repeated recycling processes. sections.heading: Alloying and Casting Experiments
paragraphs: Alloy production was conducted via a resistance-heated crucible furnace in a clay-graphite crucible with a maximum capacity of 220 kg. The AlSi7Mg0.3 master alloy was molten and heated to 740 °C. The chemical composition was controlled by optical emission spectroscopy FoundryMasterPro2, Hitachi. Grain refinement was conducted with AlTi5B1 master alloy. Additionally, the to-be-investigated elements Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn were added, using technical pure metals (Zn and Cu), respectively AlFe80 and AlMn80 master alloys. Degassing was done by a rotary degassing unit, using N 2 , aiming for a density index of less than 2.0 %. Finally, melt refinement with AlSr10 master alloy was undertaken. If necessary, Mg99.9 was added to compensate for burn-up losses. The final composition of each variant is shown in Table  3 . All experiments were cast manually in a permanent steel mold for tensile specimen whose cavity is schematically shown in Figure  1 . The mold was pre-heated using heating cartridges and held at ca. 320 °C for each cast. The casting temperature was 720 °C ± 10 °C. sections.heading: Analysis Methods
paragraphs: The specimens taken from the heat-treated cast samples were then analyzed microscopically and mechanically. Furthermore, corrosion testing was performed.

sections.heading: Microscopy
paragraphs: Specimen taken from heat-treated samples and corrosion tests were ground and polished and analyzed in an Olympus BX53M optical microscope. Furthermore, analyses of fractured surfaces of notched specimen fatigue tests for each configuration were conducted with a Hitachi S-3400N SEM.

sections.heading: Corrosion Testing
paragraphs: Corrosion tests were performed on defined parts of the gating system (as shown in Figure  1 ) in an alternating immersion test according to DIN 50905-4, 18  where a 3% sodium chloride solution has been used. The specimens underwent 900 alternating immersion cycles in a 3 % sodium chloride solution: 5 min immersion followed by 25 min drying above the solution level. For the assessment, the specimens were weighed by a laboratory balance with an accuracy of ± 0.001 g. Based on this, we quantified the amount of corrosion products formed.

sections.heading: Tensile Tests
paragraphs: In order to obtain a detailed influence of the alloying elements on the mechanical properties, a wide range of tensile test types was performed to analyze different stress states and loading conditions. Conventional tensile tests with two different specimen sizes, dynamic tensile tests at elevated loading rates, as well as notched tensile tests and torsion tests under quasi-static conditions were performed. The specimens were extracted from the casting bars as illustrated by Figure  2 . The extraction positions of all specimens were carefully documented and the positions of the specimens (gate-adjacent) have been shuffled to create variation in terms of possible porosity within the test series.

sections.heading: Cyclic Properties
paragraphs: Approximately, 15 test series comprising a total of 68 specimens were conducted on AlSi7Mg0.3 to evaluate its fatigue behavior under force- and strain-controlled loading conditions. The cyclic test data were statistically evaluated using the maximum likelihood method, following the approach described in Störzel and Baumgartner. 22  The slope   k * after the knee point was set to 22 for cast aluminum alloys, following the recommendation by Sonsino. 23

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs: This section reports the results of microstructural and defect analyses and discusses the findings from quasi-static, dynamic and fatigue testing.

sections.heading: Defect Analysis of Individual Tensile Test Specimens
paragraphs: A manual analysis of the scanned cast bars was performed by Fraunhofer IWM in order to correlate the results with the obtained mechanical properties from quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests. The manual analysis was necessary because relevant defects need to be located within the extracted specimen and the strained volume. The data was manually analyzed like shown in Figure  7 . The specimens were largely free of defects within the detection limits of the scans. In contrast, the smaller specimens (6 mm diameter) from materials S1 and S3 exhibited considerable variability. Figure 7 Illustration of manual extraction of relevant defects within a tensile test specimen.

paragraphs: Obviously, copper has the biggest impact on corrosion behavior of A356 aluminum alloy. Figure  8  presents the mass of the corrosion products. Although the number of specimens was restricted by the test-chamber capacity, the observed trends were reproducible across the available samples and are meaningful within the study’s constraints. sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: This section covers the quasi-static and dynamic properties, with results presented and discussed. Torsion tests were carried out and are described in this chapter. The study is concluded by the fatigue behavior of the three configurations, which completes the investigation of the contaminated alloys.

sections.heading: Quasi-Static and Dynamic Tensile Test Properties
paragraphs: Under dynamic loading conditions, a substantial increase in  R p 0.2  is observed, while  R m  rises moderately and only slightly in S3 (Figure  12 ). Simultaneously, A g  (Uniform Elongation) decreases, whereas A 5  (Elongation at Break) increases significantly in S1 and S3 and slightly in S2. This behavior suggests that adiabatic heating during deformation plays a role in enhancing ductility. The scatter in A g  and A 5  appears smaller at elevated loading rates compared to quasi-static testing, but this is most likely connected to differences in porosity and not a consequence of the testing conditions, as elaborated later. Since heat conduction is a time-dependent process, the temperature in the specimen increases significantly due to the decreased testing time at elevated loading rates. The result is a local temperature gradient that can severely impact mechanical properties, most notably increasing ductility at the end of the loading process. This was also observed in this paper, most notably for S1 and S3. As analyzed in detail by 25  for a pressure vessel steel, strain rates of 100 /s can produce temperature increases of over 100 K in the highly deformed region, resulting in a significant increase in ductility. The increased elongation at fracture or ductility with increased loading rate is also commonly observed in other materials. 26 , 27  also observed this phenomenon for 7XXX wrought alloys. 5XXX-alloys with higher Mg-content show an even stronger increase in ductility, since the Portevin-Le-Chatelier (PLC) -effect is neutralized with higher loading rates as observed by Andrieux et al. 28  Since the Mg-content is very low in the present materials and no PLC-effect was observed under quasi-static testing conditions, the neutralization of this phenomenon with increased loading rate can be ruled out.

The determined elongation at fracture A 5  is also shown as a function of the number of detected and maximum defects within the individual specimens in Figures  13  and  14 . Especially under quasi-static conditions and for small specimens, higher defect number and size are associated with a decrease in ductility. This can be used to explain the higher scatter in the test series for S1 and S3 compared to S2, which had no detectable porosity. This statement is strengthened by data from the large specimens in Figure  14 , since the materials here showed almost no porosity and consequently much less scatter in mechanical response. A 5 -values of defect-free specimens of both specimen sizes are very similar. Analogous observations and conclusions can be made regarding maximum defect size. Furthermore, the specimen used for dynamic testing conditions showed only very few casting defects, so an impact under elevated loading rates could not be determined in this study. The scatter here, however, was quite low, which is in line with the observations and statements made for quasi-static testing conditions. Figure 13 Quasi-static mechanical properties vs. number of defects and maximum defect radius within the individual specimens (  d  = 6 mm). Figure 14 Quasi-static mechanical properties vs. number of defects and maximum defect radius within the individual specimens (  d  = 10 mm).

sections.heading: Fatigue Behavior
Notch Sensitivity of AlSi7Mg0.3
paragraphs: Figure  16  shows the results of the notched tensile test and torsion test for the three material types. In general, very similar influences of the alloying elements can be observed as already stated for the conventional quasi-static tensile tests. The variant S2 shows significant reduction in ductility in the form of displacement and maximum torque angle DIC, whereas the influence under torsion appears to be less severe compared to the notched or conventional tensile tests. A further reduction in ductility is not observed regarding S3, which slightly contrasts the observations from the conventional tensile tests. Strength, however, is slightly increased in S2 but reduced back to levels of S1 for S3. Figure 16 left: results of notched tensile test; right: results of torsion test for test bars in heat-treated state (T64).

sections.heading: Fracture Surface Analysis
paragraphs: A selection of representative fracture modes of notched fatigue specimen for the three investigated material variants is presented in Figure  18 . The primary alloy (configuration S1 AlSi7Mg0.3) shows damage initiation either at casting defects such as shrinkage pores or from the surface. For configuration S2 (AlSi7Mg0.3 + Fe0.5 + Mn0.25), a network of iron-rich phases becomes visible, which appears bright in the BSE (backscattered electron contrast) image. In some cases, individual needle-shaped phases can be found. Finally for configuration S3 (AlSi7Mg0.3 + Fe0.5 + Mn0.25 + Cu0.35 + Zn0.2) clusters of needle-shaped or larger phases are present at the fracture surface. However, for both S2 and S3 configuration, even if the fracture initiation zone features larger amounts of secondary phases, it is not proven that fracture is initiated by the secondary phases. This is supported by the results of the fatigue testing (Figure  17 ) where the SN curves show a similar or even slightly increased fatigue strength for material variants S2 and S3 compared to the primary alloy S1. Figure 18 Selection of representative fracture surfaces of notched fatigue specimens after testing: Configuration S1 (AlSi7Mg0.3 primary): Damage initiation from shrinkage pores and casting defects (1a) or surface (1b) / Configuration S2 (AlSi7Mg0.3 + Fe0.5 + Mn0.25): Network of secondary phases visible at fracture surface (2a) and needle-shaped Fe-rich phases (2b) / Configuration S3 (AlSi7Mg0.3 + Fe0.5 + Mn0.25 + Cu0.35 + Zn0.2): Fe-rich phases visible at fracture surface: needle shaped (3a) or larger areas (3b).

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: In summary, the alloy variants S2 and S3 exhibit improved fatigue strength compared to the primary alloy S1, but at the cost of ductility. Tensile tests revealed that the additional alloying elements fundamentally alter mechanical properties. The addition of + Fe and Mn leads to a significant decrease in ductility or elongation at fracture  A 5 , while the addition of + Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn results in a further, albeit smaller, decrease. These observations can be attributed to the additional elements, while the observed scatter is clearly linked to detected casting defects in the material. S3 appears to offer the best combination of strength and fatigue resistance, whereas S2 shows a significant reduction in ductility. It was found that the addition of Fe and Mn has no impact on corrosion properties, while higher concentrations of Cu lead to a significant deterioration. This aligns with existing literature, emphasizing that Cu additions in corrosion-prone aluminum components should be avoided. Ductility increases significantly at elevated loading rates for S1 and S3, and slightly for S2. The influence of loading type and stress state (notched tensile and torsion tests) did not reveal major differences regarding the effects of the alloying elements.
